questions.prompt: On Android, what happens to an Activity when the device is rotated, by default?

options.text: It is paused but never destroyed
Nothing; the Activity keeps running untouched
It is destroyed and recreated
Only the layout is re-measured

questions.explanation: A rotation is a configuration change, so the Activity is destroyed and recreated to pick up new resources. State must be preserved with a ViewModel or onSaveInstanceState.

questions.prompt: In Swift, what is the key difference between a struct and a class?

options.text: Structs are value types; classes are reference types
Structs cannot have methods
Structs are always stored on the heap
Classes cannot conform to protocols

questions.explanation: A struct is copied on assignment, while a class passes a reference to shared storage. This is why mutating a copied struct never affects the original.

questions.prompt: In Flutter, why does marking a widget's constructor as const help performance?

options.text: It lets Flutter skip rebuilding that subtree
It caches the widget's network calls
It moves the widget off the main isolate
It compiles the widget to native code

questions.explanation: A const widget is canonicalised at compile time, so the framework can recognise it as unchanged and skip rebuilding and re-laying out that subtree.

questions.prompt: What is the main cause of a retain cycle in Swift?

options.text: Using too many optionals
Force-unwrapping a nil value
Declaring variables with var instead of let
Two objects holding strong references to each other

questions.explanation: ARC frees an object when its strong reference count hits zero. If two objects reference each other strongly, neither count reaches zero and both leak. Break it with weak or unowned.

questions.prompt: In React Native, what does the bridge do?

options.text: Compiles JavaScript into Java and Objective-C
Passes serialised messages between JavaScript and native code
Renders the UI inside a WebView
Synchronises state with the backend

questions.explanation: JavaScript and native run in separate contexts and communicate by passing serialised, asynchronous messages. Chatty traffic across that boundary is a common source of jank.

questions.prompt: Why does an Android ViewModel survive a screen rotation?

options.text: It is a singleton shared across the whole app
It runs on a background thread
It is stored in SharedPreferences automatically
It is scoped to the Activity's lifecycle owner, not the instance

questions.explanation: The ViewModel is retained across configuration changes because it is scoped to the lifecycle owner rather than to the destroyed Activity instance. It is cleared when the owner finishes for good.

questions.prompt: In SwiftUI, when should you use @StateObject rather than @ObservedObject?

options.text: When the object is passed in from a parent
They are interchangeable in all cases
When the view creates and owns the object
Only for objects stored in UserDefaults

questions.explanation: @StateObject makes the view the owner, so the object survives view re-creation. @ObservedObject on a view-created object would be re-instantiated on every redraw, silently resetting its state.

questions.prompt: In Flutter, what problem do Keys solve in a list of widgets?

options.text: They encrypt data passed between screens
They let the framework match widgets to the right state when items move
They uniquely identify routes for navigation
They make scrolling smoother by caching images

questions.explanation: Without keys, Flutter matches widgets by position and type, so reordering or deleting an item can attach the wrong State to the wrong widget. A key ties state to identity instead.

questions.prompt: Which best describes an ANR on Android?

options.text: The app exceeded its memory limit
The main thread was blocked too long to respond to input
The app was denied a runtime permission
A network request timed out

questions.explanation: An Application Not Responding dialog appears when the main thread is blocked past a threshold, usually by disk or network work that should have been moved off it.

questions.prompt: In Kotlin coroutines, what does structured concurrency give you?

options.text: Child coroutines are cancelled when their scope is cancelled
Coroutines run in parallel on separate CPU cores
Every coroutine runs on the main thread
Exceptions are silently swallowed

questions.explanation: Coroutines launched in a scope are children of it, so cancelling the scope cancels them all. This is what stops work leaking after a screen is destroyed.

questions.prompt: Why is [weak self] commonly used inside an escaping closure in Swift?

options.text: To allow the closure to mutate self
To let the closure run on a background thread
To make the closure execute faster
To stop the closure keeping self alive and creating a cycle

questions.explanation: An escaping closure stored on an object captures self strongly by default, so the object holds the closure and the closure holds the object. Capturing weakly breaks that cycle.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of Android's RecyclerView ViewHolder pattern?

options.text: It avoids repeated view lookups by caching references
It stores list data in a database
It sorts the list automatically
It renders the list on the GPU

questions.explanation: The ViewHolder holds direct references to a row's views, so scrolling reuses recycled rows instead of inflating layouts and calling findViewById repeatedly.

questions.prompt: In Dart, what does async/await actually do?

options.text: Runs the function on a separate thread
Forces the code to run synchronously
Spawns a new isolate per call
Suspends the function until a Future completes, without blocking the isolate

questions.explanation: Dart is single-threaded per isolate. await suspends the function and returns control to the event loop, resuming when the Future completes. Heavy CPU work still needs a separate isolate.

questions.prompt: Which of these can NOT be shipped through a React Native over-the-air update?

options.text: An updated image bundled with the JS
A bug fix in business logic
A newly added native module
A change to a JavaScript component

questions.explanation: OTA updates replace the JavaScript bundle and its assets. Anything requiring recompiled native code, such as a new native module, needs a full store release.

questions.prompt: In SwiftUI, what does @State exist for?

options.text: Injecting dependencies into child views
Persisting values to disk between launches
Sharing state across the whole app
Local, view-owned value state that triggers a redraw when it changes

questions.explanation: @State stores small, view-local value state outside the struct so it survives redraws, and invalidates the body when it changes. Shared reference state belongs in @StateObject or @Observable.

questions.prompt: Why is it bad practice to do long-running work inside an Android BroadcastReceiver's onReceive?

options.text: onReceive cannot access the file system
Broadcasts are delivered only once per day
It runs on the main thread and the receiver is short-lived
onReceive cannot start any other component

questions.explanation: onReceive runs on the main thread and the receiver is considered finished when it returns, so long work blocks the UI and may be killed. Hand off to WorkManager or a service.

questions.prompt: What does Jetpack Compose recomposition mean?

options.text: The app process restarts
The layout file is re-parsed from XML
The navigation stack is rebuilt
Composables re-run because state they read changed

questions.explanation: Compose tracks which state each composable reads and re-runs only those that depend on changed state. Reading state too high in the tree causes unnecessary recomposition.

questions.prompt: In iOS, why must UI updates happen on the main thread?

options.text: The GPU only accepts commands from the main thread
UIKit and SwiftUI are not thread-safe
It makes animations run faster
Background threads have no memory access

questions.explanation: The UI frameworks assume single-threaded access. Touching views from a background thread causes intermittent corruption and crashes, which is why the main actor exists in Swift concurrency.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of Flutter's own rendering engine over using native widgets?

options.text: It makes network calls faster
It removes the need for platform-specific code entirely
It guarantees smaller app binaries
It gives identical pixel output across platforms

questions.explanation: Flutter draws every pixel itself with Skia, so a screen looks the same everywhere. The cost is a larger binary and UI that does not automatically match platform conventions.

questions.prompt: What is the correct fix for a flaky test that only passes when you add a fixed sleep before tapping a button?

options.text: Wait for an explicit condition, such as the button becoming enabled
Retry the whole test three times
Disable the test on slower devices
Increase the sleep until it stops failing

questions.explanation: A sleep encodes a guess about timing and breaks on a slower machine. Waiting on the actual condition removes the race rather than hiding it.

questions.prompt: Which storage option is appropriate for a user's authentication token on mobile?

options.text: An in-memory variable only
The Keychain on iOS or EncryptedSharedPreferences on Android
A hardcoded constant in the source
SharedPreferences or UserDefaults in plain text

questions.explanation: Preferences files are plain text and readable from a backup or a rooted device. The Keychain and EncryptedSharedPreferences are backed by the platform's secure storage.

questions.prompt: In Flutter, what does setState do?

options.text: Persists the widget's state to disk
Pushes a new route onto the navigator
Marks the widget dirty so its build method runs again
Rebuilds the entire widget tree from the root

questions.explanation: setState notifies the framework that this State object changed, scheduling a rebuild of that widget's subtree only, not the whole app.

questions.prompt: Why does a mobile app usually paginate a long list from the server instead of fetching everything?

options.text: Pagination is required by the app stores
It makes the data more secure
It reduces memory use, data cost and time to first render
Servers cannot return large JSON responses

questions.explanation: Devices have limited memory and users are often on metered, slow connections. Paging keeps the first screen fast and avoids holding thousands of rows in memory.

questions.prompt: On Android, what is the difference between StateFlow and LiveData for exposing UI state?

options.text: LiveData works only in Compose
StateFlow is a coroutines primitive and always has a value; LiveData is lifecycle-aware by design
StateFlow cannot hold a current value
They are the same class with different names

questions.explanation: StateFlow comes from coroutines and always holds a current value, but collection must be tied to the lifecycle manually. LiveData was built around lifecycle awareness from the start.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a mobile app to work offline-first?

options.text: The app reads and writes locally, then syncs when a connection returns
The app disables all features until it is online
The app refuses to launch without a network connection
All data is stored only on the server

questions.explanation: Offline-first treats the local store as the source of truth for the session, so the UI stays responsive without a connection and reconciles with the server later.
